tagline: A highway with no centerline, kept that way on purpose.
intro: Out of Harbor Springs on Bluff Drive, M-119 turns north along the Lake Michigan shore and narrows into the woods, oak and maple, birch and cedar, on an old Odawa trail along the bluffs. The lake shows only now and then through the trees. Twenty miles on it comes out at Cross Village.

In 1936, when there was talk of widening it for traffic, Alice Irwin took up the road's cause in her newspaper column and petitioned the Legislature to keep it as it was. It still has no shoulders and no centerline.

moments.title: Devil's Elbow
moments.text: North of the Hoogland preserve the road makes one sharp turn, a named spot on a road that is mostly curves anyway.

moments.title: Good Hart
moments.text: Middle Village, halfway along, was once an Ojibwe settlement led by Joseph Black Hawk and his brother Good Heart. Its 1934 general store is still open and keeps the post office.

moments.title: Cross Village
moments.text: High on a bluff over the lake, where Legs Inn, built in 1921, takes its name from the stove legs set along its roofline.

practical: The road is narrow and winding with low branches, hard going for large vehicles. There is no fuel between Harbor Springs and Cross Village and very few public restrooms.
